## Appendix A

With appropriate data, the drone energy consumption rate Epm can be calculated as

$$
E p m = \frac {\text {BatteryEnergy}}{\text {FlightDistance}}\tag{A1}
$$

Information on the BatteryEnergy is often, but not always, provided by the manufacturer; either in Watt-hours (1 Wh = 3600 J) or as capacity and voltage, where

$$
B a t t e r y E n e r g y (i n J) = C a p a c i t y (i n m A h) \times V o l t a g e (i n V) \times 3. 6.\tag{A2}
$$

However, FlightDistance information is not reported by all manufacturers, nor is it provided in a consistent manner. Flight distance data from manufacturer websites may be the distance under conditions that maximize that distance (e.g., the speed, altitude and weather conditions that maximize distance) and do not reflect real-world drone operations. We are aware of only a few drones for which flight distance at an associated speed is reported (see Table A1). As most manufacturers report a flight time or hovering time and a maximum speed for each drone, it is tempting to use that data to estimate flight distance as

$$
\text {FlightDistance} = \text {FlightSpeed} \times \text {FlightTime}\tag{A3}
$$

Yet, because manufacturers often report a maximum value (e.g., “Max Flight Time” or “Max Speed”) or an unspecified value (e.g., “Flight Time”), and drone energy use depends strongly on speed, combining a maximum flight (or hovering) time with a maximum speed is likely to provide an inaccurate flight distance measure. Thus, the seemingly straightforward approach of FlightSpeed × FlightTime is fraught with uncertainties due to unclear and inconsistent reporting of information by different manufacturers, as well as inconsistencies across drones for the same manufacturer.

As an example of the difficulties, consider the data below for DJI drones in the first 5 rows of Table A1 (from [https://www.dji.com/products/compare-consumer-drones](https://www.dji.com/products/compare-consumer-drones)), which provides “Max Flight Time” at a particular speed (see column 3), along with “Max Hovering Time”, “Max Speed” and “Max Flight Distance” (see columns 4–6). The flight distance calculated based on the time and speed in column 3 using eq. (A3) is shown in column 7, and the flight distance calculated based on the hovering time (column 5) and maximum speed (column 6) (using eq. (A3) with hovering time) is shown in column 8. Note that the three flight distance values in columns 6–8 disagree considerably. It is not surprising that column 8 is much greater than the flight distance in column 6 (on average about twice as large), because high speeds increase the rate of energy consumption which would reduce the endurance at that maximum speed to well below the hovering time. It may also not be surprising that the distances calculated in column 7 (based on the speed and time from column 3) are much less (13%-40% less) than the reported flight distance in column 6, if the column 6 values are based on the distance-maximizing speed (while column 3 may report the typical operational speed; and we note speeds of 5–6 m/s are typical for imaging applications). This illustrates the need to use common data elements, and the dangers of combining different calculations of flight distance across different manufacturers.

We do not include values for other DJI drones (Inspire, the Matrice series, and the Agricultural drones AGRAS T-16 and the MG series) in Table A1, as the website does not provide flight distances for its other drones (only the maximum flight or hovering time and maximum speed). We were able to collect relevant data for 2 other drones from manufacturer websites, as shown in the last two rows of Table A1 for the Microdrones MD4-3000 and the 3D Robotics 3DR-Solo. Thus, Table A1 includes data for three manufacturers where both flight distance and battery energy information was reported. Columns 2–6 and 9 are from the manufacturer websites. Column 9 is the battery energy, either provided directly or calculated based on capacity (mAh) × voltage. Columns 7 and 8 are calculated flight distances for the DJI drones as described above. Column 10 is the Epm calculated using equation (A1) (column 9 divided by column 6).

Because of the issues illustrated above for the DJI drones, we are hesitant to recommend computing energy consumption rates using manufacturer data unless the drone operating conditions are clearly specified and they match the particular application of interest (e. g., imaging may require slower speeds than delivery). We also note that energy consumption rates calculated with manufacturer data using a takeoff weight with no payload is not directly comparable to energy consumption rates in the literature for delivery drones carrying a payload. Finally, we also note that some researchers reduce the battery energy available for flight or the travel distance to reflect operating realities. For example, Figliozzi (2017) assumes for one of his analyses that the drone flight range is only 70% of the maximum flight distance to account for unknown factors (e.g., bad weather) that increase energy consumption and to provide a safety margin. To achieve a similar goal, Stolaroff et al. (2018) and Troudi et al. (2018) assume a safety factor of 1.2 and 1.25, respectively, to reserve energy for unusual conditions (which is equivalent to using 83.3% and 80% of maximum flight distance, respectively).

## Appendix B

This appendix provides a derivation of the energy consumption for a battery powered aircraft in steady level flight (i.e. at a constant altitude and constant speed), as in D’Andrea (2014), based on fundamental principles of flight. Four fundamental forces acting on an aircraft in steady flight are thrust to move forward, weight from gravity acting on the aircraft mass, lift in the direction opposing gravity, and drag in the direction opposing travel (from aerodynamic effects of the shape of the aircraft, such as friction with air). The amount of energy in joules needed to fly a distance d (measured in meters) at constant altitude can be modeled as

$$
E _ {f l y} = T \times d\tag{B1}
$$

where T is the thrust force measured in Newtons $(\mathrm{kg} - \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{sec}^2)$ . Note that this does not account for the energy involved with the vertical travel components to lift the aircraft from the ground to a cruising altitude and to lower it back to the ground. For drone delivery, this may occur twice each trip, once at takeoff/landing and once for the delivery; however, drone deliveries may not require landing, as the package may be lowed via a tether or dropped via parachute.

An important factor for aircraft performance is the lift-to-drag ratio $r ,$ a unitless parameter which captures the efficiency of the aircraft design in keeping the aircraft airborne. Values of the lift-to-drag ratio range widely from about 10–20 for commercial passenger aircraft to about 4 for helicopters in cruising flight, to typically smaller values for UAV rotocopters. The lift-to-drag ratio varies with aircraft speed due to drag and the aerodynamic affects from lifting surfaces, but is constant in steady flight. To keep the aircraft in steady flight, lift is equal to weight and thrust is equal to drag, so

$$
\boxed {T = d r a g = \frac {\text {lift}}{r} = \frac {\text {weight}}{r} = \frac {\text {mass} \times g}{r}}\tag{B2}
$$

where $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity (9.8 m/sec<sup>2</sup>) and mass is the total weight of the aircraft (body, battery and payload) in kg. Combining (B1) and (B2) gives

$$
E _ {f l y} = \frac {\left(m _ {1} + m _ {2} + m _ {3}\right) \times g}{r} \times d\tag{B3}
$$

where $m _ { 1 } \mathbf { i } \mathbf { s }$ the mass of the aircraft structure, $m _ { 2 }$ is the mass of the aircraft battery and $m _ { 3 }$ is the mass of the payload.

An important parameter for battery powered drones is the efficiency for converting battery power to “flight” power delivered by the rotors, denoted η (unitless), whereη $< 1$ . Thus, the energy required from the battery for steady flight is

$$
E _ {f l y} = \frac {\left(m _ {1} + m _ {2} + m _ {3}\right) \times g}{\eta r} \times d\tag{B4}
$$

Additional energy is consumed by the drone avionics required for safe flight, including communications, sensing, computation, etc. Let $P _ { a v i o }$ be the power required for the aircraft (drone) avionics in joules per second of flight. The energy for avionics (in joules) for a flight of distance d is then

$$
E _ {a v i o} = P _ {a v i o} \times \frac {d}{v}\tag{B5}
$$

The total energy expended by the aircraft battery (in joules) on a flight of distance d is from equations (B4) and (B5):

$$
E _ {t o t} = \frac {\left(m _ {1} + m _ {2} + m _ {3}\right) g}{r \eta} d + P _ {a v i o} \times \frac {d}{v}\tag{B6}
$$

The total energy expended per meter of flight Epm is then

$$
\boxed {E p m = \frac {\left(m _ {1} + m _ {2} + m _ {3}\right) g}{r \eta} + \frac {P _ {a v i o}}{v}}\tag{B7}
$$

This is equivalent to the formula presented in D’Andrea (2014) for power

$$
\frac {(m _ {1} + m _ {2} + m _ {3}) v}{3 7 0 r \eta} + P _ {\text {avio}}
$$

because power equals $\mathit { E p m } \times \nu ,$ and the constant 370 in the denominator of the first term results from substituting in 9.81 for g and measuring speed in km/hr rather than m/sec (3600/9.81 = 367).

## Appendix C

The model in Kirchstein (2020) for steady flight is based on the power model in Langelaan et al. (2017) where the power for constant speed flight includes four components for: induced power for lift, power to overcome parasite drag, profile power, and ascending/descending power (based on flight angle θ). This is expressed as a function of the mass and flight angle:

$$
P \left(m _ {k}, v _ {a}, \gamma\right) = \kappa w T + \frac {1}{2} \rho \left(\sum_ {k = 1} ^ {3} C _ {D _ {k}} A _ {k}\right) v _ {a} ^ {3} + \frac {\rho \sqrt {\varsigma / \pi} n N c c _ {d}}{8} v _ {T} ^ {3} \left(1 + 3 \left(\frac {v _ {a}}{v _ {T}}\right) ^ {2}\right) + \left(g \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {3} m _ {k}\right) v _ {a} \sin \theta\tag{C1}
$$

where $v_{T} = \sqrt{\frac{6}{nNcc_{l}\rho\sqrt{\varsigma/\pi}}}\sqrt{g\sum_{k = 1}^{3}m_{k}}$ is the blade tip speed. The parameter $w ,$ like the induced velocity in Stolaroff et al. (2018), is found by solving the following equation

$$
w = \frac {T}{2 n \rho \varsigma \sqrt {\left(v _ {a} \cos \alpha\right) ^ {2} + \left(v _ {a} \sin \alpha + w\right) ^ {2}}}\tag{C2}
$$

where T is from equation (20) and α is from equation (15).

The energy per meter for steady level flight $( \theta = 0 )$ for a total drone mass of m (including battery and payload if any) with avionics power $P _ { a v i o }$ is

$$
E p m = \frac {P (m , v _ {a} , 0)}{\eta v _ {a}} + \frac {P _ {a v i o}}{\eta_ {c} v _ {a}}\tag{C3}
$$

Kirchstein (2020) uses a total energy efficiency η for drone flight power that includes the motor, transmission and battery charging efficiency, but only the charging efficiency $\eta _ { c }$ for the avionics.

For a delivery by a drone moving at speed $\nu _ { a }$ with no wind to a distance d from the depot, the total energy including take-off and ascent at $4 5 ^ { \circ }$ to an altitude of alt, level flight, hovering for time $t _ { h o v e r : }$ and then landing, is

$$
\begin{array}{l} E p m = \frac {1}{v _ {a}} \left[ \frac {P (m , v _ {a} , 0)}{\eta} + \frac {P _ {a v i o}}{\eta_ {c}} \right] + \frac {1}{v _ {a}} \frac {a l t}{d} \frac {1}{\eta} \left[ P (m, v _ {a}, 4 5 ^ {\circ}) + P (m, v _ {a}, - 4 5 ^ {\circ}) - 2 P (m, v _ {a}, 0) \right] \\ + \frac {t _ {h o v e r}}{d} \left[ \frac {P (m , 0 , 0)}{\eta} + \frac {P _ {a v i o}}{\eta_ {c}} \right] \end{array}\tag{C4}
$$

The return trip would be the same, but without the payload $(m = m_{1} + m_{2})$ . The first term in (C4) is for the level flight, which will usually be the majority of the trip (unless the delivery is for a very short distance), the second term is for the ascending and descending, and the last term is for hovering.
